## Investors pile in - then out - of copper Comex non-commercial futures and options, Jan 2010-Sep 2011 ## So turbulence ahead... - Heading into LME Week, there are **more questions than answers** over the macroeconomic/financial outlook and its potential impact on the copper market. - The **key issues** facing the industry against this backdrop of turbulence and commodity price volatility are: - **the implications for demand** - **the implications for supply; project financing, high cost production and scrap** - **comparisons to 2008; what remains the same, and what has changed** - Market fundamentals showed few signs of the impending price correction. Copper demand growth has held up well this year, with latest estimates suggesting a 3% increase y-o-y. **Exchange stocks have failed to build** significantly while mine production has experienced **disruptions** from ore grade declines, strikes and poor weather conditions. - Given the latest state of affairs, the key change since our July Quarterly, has been the minor revi

sion downward to our consumption outlook and as a consequence we now estimate a **global market deficit of 140,000t in 2011** . ## ...but is there worse to come? Part I - We are in no doubt that there will be comparisons to the 2008 financial crisis but we do believe that **copper is unlikely to suffer the same losses** . There are some **key differences** : - The **copper stock pipeline remains very lean** across the entire supply chain. Inventories of both concentrates and cathode have been drawn down, particularly in China where we believe there was build up in stock by the end of 2010. Consumers in the rest of the world have been very reluctant to build up any more inventory than required given the clouded outlook for end-use requirements. - The majority of the **projects** that are due to come on stream in the near term are inherently **less risky brownfield sites.** Many of these are owned by the majors who are flush with cash and so the impact of potential financial tightening is diminished. It is not until 2013 that greenfield projects begin to dominate the growth in mine supply and by then the clouds will have surely lifted. ## Projects could provide more than 8Mt/y of copper by 2016 **Forecast vs. potential production from all mine projects** 9,000 projects

## ...but is there worse to come? Part II There are some other key differences: • **Lessons have been learnt** from the 2008/2009 crash in copper prices and it is now **much more difficult to renege on scrap** . That said, in the short term any merchants holding on to scrap bought at the higher prices will hold on to that material until they feel prices are unlikely to recover so will then have to accept the loss. In the mean time that scrap will have to be replaced, either by cathode (if scrap no.1) or by concentrate (low grades). This should provide some support to prices. - Despite the macro economic and financial whirlwind that is currently in full swing, **refined copper is now 25% more affordable** than it was on 1st August. This is a big factor for those price sensitive national buyers (China, India, Brazil) and government stockpiles (SRB, KPPC). Chinese net refined imports reached 235kt in August. This is the highest level so far this year. Will China save the copper market once again? - Moreover, copper’s key end-use market, **wire and cable has very diverse applications** and is unlikely to be derailed unless there is a global slump into a deep recession. Indeed at $7,500/t this could be a good time to buy wire and cable. ## Disruptions at mines much higher than expected in H1 this year Mine output change 2010 to 2011, copper in concs and EW cathode Mine output change

## ...but is there worse to come? Part III • **There was an unprecedented level of disruptions in Q2 & Q3 2011.** These have not gone away. The continuing problem of **declining ore grades** and **infrastructure constraints** , especially in Zambia and Chile are not going to be resolved quickly. Although some **labour disruptions** were directly related to the high price, others centred around demands for better working conditions. • **Resource nationalism** remains a key threat for producers, particularly in places like Peru, Mongolia and the DRC where many new projects are due to come through. All these factors should provide some support to prices. Gap between operating costs and prices will

*143 operations covering 90% of global copper production ## Consumption - but fears for future Part I - As yet there are **no direct signs that the turbulence has had a direct impact on** . - **physical copper demand** - What is apparent however is that the consumers are likely to wait as long as possible before they commit to volumes for their 2012 contracts with the producers in the hope of some clarity emerging. - Although the **emerging markets are performing well** , driven by domestic demand, there is some concern about inflationary pressure in these countries. Governments will have to weigh up these pressures against the impact of economic contraction. - China is a third of the world, and 40% of global copper demand. So if it continues to grow, as looks likely even if it is at a slower rate, this is a big positive for global demand. Our assumptions suggest that over the balance of 2011 they will have to import an average of **200,000tpm** to feed demand. In 2012, the implicit deficit on refined . - consumption and output should see average refined imports of **100,000-150,000tpm** - At these lower prices some Chinese consumers or the SRB could see **copper as a bargain** for speculative purposes! Data: GTIS, Antaike, Company Reports, CRU ## Consumption - but fears for future Part II - Further support for copper could emerge from participants wishing to steer some of their cash, (and we include the Chinese) away from the dollar and into commodity investments as a means of diversification. - Japan is recovering slightly faster than we anticipated this year and looking ahead should post growth of 4% in 2012. - The developing countries of the world continue to look strong, supported by infrastructure development which is typically large government funded projects. **China** and the other BRIC’s, **India** , **Brazil** , **Russia** are still growing and the **GCC** has lots of oil money and is still investing, particularly **Saudi Arabia** . - • One area of concern is the USA where Russian rod imports are depressing US refined consumption, irrespective of the economic outlook. The economic background is unresolved There are some other key differences yet the key questions remain: - How long will it take to sort out the European debt crisis? _This is in reality only something that the politicians can answer._ - What will be the impact on industrial output growth? _We have tried to present our assessment of the situation and the impact on the copper market in particular. However it will very much depend on how long the world remains held up in the eye of this storm!_ ### **Risks to the demand outlook** - Potential impact of political turmoil resulting in financial market stress and **another serious recession in the Euro zone and the USA** . - Longer term the **substitution threat** remains significant for copper demand growth _._ - **_BUT_** - **The potential shortage of scrap** (due to weaker generation) during a double dip and the impact, if any, on additional cathode requirements (especially China). - The extent that the **emerging markets** have been able to **decouple growth from** the **industrialised countries** . ### **Risks to the supply outlook** - Potential impact of political turmoil resulting in financial market stress and **another serious recession in the Euro zone and the USA** on the availability of financing for the projects due on stream over the next five years. - Availability of equipment, qualified personnel, water, power etc. mean that the sequencing of projects (at both the company and industry levels) will be a serious challenge for the unprecedented forecast growth in refined production in 2014 and 2015 to be achieved. - **The potential shortage of scrap** (due to weaker generation) during a double dip and the impact, if any, on smelters and their increased reliance on concentrates.
